title: The hour has come (John 17:1–5)
hook: he lifts his eyes and prays for the Father's glory

segments.voice: Yesterday, a woman in labor, and words spoken before the victory showed. Your line was be of good cheer. How did your trouble look with courage beside it? Day six hundred thirty-nine.

For three chapters Jesus has been talking to his friends. Now, suddenly, he stops talking to them and starts talking to God, out loud, while they listen. The prayer fills the whole of John seventeen. Christians often call it the High Priestly Prayer, because in it he stands between God and his friends, the way a priest does. And it starts with a small physical detail John doesn't want you to miss. He looks up.

In the King James Bible: "These words spake Jesus, and lifted up his eyes to heaven, and said, Father, the hour is come; glorify thy Son, that thy Son also may glorify thee." John has shown this before: at Lazarus's tomb, too, Jesus lifted up his eyes and said, Father. And then the first words: the hour is come. If you've been reading John from the start, that line lands hard. At the wedding at Cana, Jesus told his mother, mine hour is not yet come. More than once, people tried to seize him, and they couldn't, John says, because his hour had not yet come. Then, a few chapters back, when some Greeks came looking for him, he said it at last: the hour is come. The whole Gospel has been counting down to this. And what is the hour for? Glory. In John, that word does something unexpected. The glory isn't a throne or a crown. In John's telling it is bound up with the cross: the moment that looks like shame is the moment John calls glory. Then comes a definition, and it's the line in today's carry: "And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent." Notice it doesn't define eternal life as living forever, or as a place you go after you die. It defines it as knowing. And knowing, in the Bible, is often close and personal: the way you know a friend, not a fact. So for John, eternal life can begin now, in a relationship, not only later.
screen: `HE LIFTS HIS EYES, AS AT LAZARUS'S TOMB.`
`NOT YET, NOT YET, AND NOW THE HOUR.`
`IN JOHN, THE GLORY IS THE CROSS.`
then, large: `FATHER, THE HOUR IS COME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: lift your eyes as you pray. If you can, stand up, or sit straight, and slowly lift your face. Look at the ceiling, or out a window at the sky. Notice how different it feels from looking down at a screen, or at the floor. Breathe there. If you pray, you can pray with your eyes lifted the way he did, even just the word Father. If you don't, simply let your eyes rest on something high and wide, and let your thoughts get bigger than the day so far. The bell holds the time.
The hour has come. The moment John's whole Gospel has been counting toward: the cross, which John calls glory.
Your line: this is life eternal. Today, spend ten unhurried minutes really getting to know someone, and notice that knowing is a kind of life. Day six hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Many churches read John 17 in the days between Ascension and Pentecost, and some Christians pray standing with eyes and hands lifted.

original.note: Greek: the hour has come. hora, the hour, is John's word for the time of the cross.

trapdoor: what you thought: the hour is just a time of day.
what it means: the moment the whole Gospel has counted down to, and John calls it glory.
what a scholar hears: 'not yet' at Cana (2:4), 'not yet' at 7:30 and 8:20, and 'the hour is come' at 12:23 and 17:1. the name 'High Priestly Prayer' is a later title, not John's.

notes: 'High Priestly Prayer' name commonly attributed to David Chytraeus (1531–1600). Confirm.
'Longest prayer of Jesus in any of the Gospels': confirm.
Standing with eyes lifted as a common Jewish posture of prayer in the period: general statement. Confirm.
'In John, the glory is the cross' is a common reading of John's glorification language (12:23–33; 13:31). Confirm phrasing.
howItsDone: John 17 in lectionaries around the Sunday after Ascension. Confirm.
Original: ἐλήλυθεν ἡ ὥρα (17:1). Confirm form.
